title: Plugin Audit: October 2026
deck: Twelve finds, six of them called Fire. This is where we check that number instead of defending it.
opening: Twelve things landed on the radar in October, published over seven days. We called six of them Fire.
That is half, and half is not a bar — it is a coin. This audit exists to say which of the six we would defend with a straight face, and which we suspect we liked because they were free.
ratioNote: We would rather write that sentence down than quietly lower what Fire means.

defended.illformed-glitch-2: Sixteen years old and still the least polite plugin here. Nothing free does that to a drum loop.
defended.u-he-zebralette-3: A free synthesizer from u-he is not a loss-leader; it is the engine they built the paid Zebra on.
defended.slate-digital-complete-access-free-colle: Sixteen plugins for nothing, and the caveats are about the account, not the tools.
defended.ujam-detunicorn: A real instrument with a real deadline. On 19 November we find out whether we miss it.
defended.d16-group-echolite: No account, no coupon, no date. That is what a freebie is supposed to feel like.
defended.the-crow-hill-company-100-year-old-piano: Recorded before anyone restored it, which is the entire point.

demoted.azazel-audio-visualcomp-2: Good, and already covered by something you probably own.
demoted.moth-production-whirl-dt: A nice idea we would not reach for twice.
demoted.air-music-technology-air-vocal-distortio: Not open yet. It cannot earn Fire from a waiting list.
demoted.gforce-software-axxess: One of a series of GForce giveaways; the series is the story, not the plugin.
demoted.gforce-software-m-tron-select-2: A good M-Tron, and a better one is free elsewhere.

mistakes: The Slate cover pointed at a checkout page instead of the product page. A reader would have been asked for money before reading a word.
The Steinberg link went to the company home page rather than the instrument. The editor caught it, not us.
The first title counted items — Six Freeware Picks — so every addition meant rewriting the headline. The month is the edition now, and the title carries the date instead.
One publication replaced October's page with a split version, throwing away what the month had already accumulated. The diagnosis was right; the cure was not.
The email pipeline was merged able to produce packages but blind to product names: 'lifetime updates' arrived as if it were a product. It is refused at the gate until that is fixed.
closing: Nothing expired in October, so the Expired badge has still never fired in production. The first honest test is 19 November, when Detunicorn runs out.
Next audit: the last Sunday of November.
